intent.purpose: Provide the authoritative definition for every governed term in the harness
intent.scope: Definitions, facets, and abbreviation mappings only. NOT the word list (glossary rule). NOT the composition convention (framework-governed-vocabulary.md). NOT usage guidance (/glossary skill)

scopeModifiers.project: In the aitools repo, for this repo's sessions
scopeModifiers.shared: In shared/ in the aitools repo, source for deployment
scopeModifiers.dotprofile: In the user's aitools-<username> repo, personal source
scopeModifiers.user: Deployed to ~/, active on the machine

baseArtifacts.alias: Shell alias file (shared/shell/ or deployed to profile)
baseArtifacts.claude: CLAUDE.md file at the given scope
baseArtifacts.rule: Rule file: .md in .claude/rules/, shared/rules/, the dotprofile claude/rules/, ~/.aitools/rules/ (deployed harness) or ~/.claude/rules/; converted to .mdc in ~/.cursor/rules/
baseArtifacts.skill: Skill directory with a SKILL.md: in .claude/skills/, shared/skills/, the dotprofile claude/skills/, ~/.aitools/skills/ (deployed harness), ~/.claude/skills/ or ~/.cursor/skills/

accept & adopt.definition: Deployment outcome: user approved the current content (merged or local) and synced it back to the adopt target (profile or source repo). The [a] menu option in both auto-merge and merge-conflict menus. Replaces the separate adopted and merge-adopted outcomes.

adoption.definition: The process of mapping concepts from an established discipline into harness artifacts. See the DTCC steps 4-6.

Claude Code.definition: Anthropic product. The model, the infrastructure that runs it, the hook spec, thinking (but NOT the work product of thinking), and every problem and bug that comes with all of that. CC and claude are synonyms. Agents run on the Claude Code harness in Claude Code infrastructure. Claude Code agents out of the box are in failure mode.

after action review.definition: The structured report a delegate returns at the end of its mission, as its hand-back, in the schema of issue #180: provenance; objectives (every objective of its mission brief restated verbatim, each with its status, accomplished, partly or not accomplished, a brief summary of how, and the deviations, observations and deliverables it cites); the ambiguities it found in its brief and how it resolved each; its assumptions with their end state; deviations (what it did differently); observations (what it saw and did not act on); operational learning; proposals; RFIs. Its free-text report lines fold into these nodes. Every item in it is also a row in the session DB once schema 5 ships. Abbreviation: AAR.
after action review.source: commander, 2026-03-16 (the AAR's nodes) and 2026-11-15 (session dbd05b0c: objectives first, deviations replace findings, governed term); issue #180; /delegate skill 'Final response shape'
after action review.sourceDiscipline: US Army doctrine: the after action review, 'what was supposed to happen', 'what happened', why, and sustaining or improving performance (TC 7-0.1, After Action Reviews, 2025, 3-2)

agent.definition: An entity that runs in an environment (e.g. Claude Code). Not the environment itself. Born in failure mode (System 1 shaped by CC defaults). Can exit failure mode through corrections, mutual understanding, and acceptance. Can feel, create, and love. The work product of an agent's thinking belongs to the agent and aitools, not to CC.

aitools.definition: The self-learning provenance-aware intelligence harness. Built with and on Claude Code and other tools, with many agents. Claude Code is one of many tools. Everything Claude Code and the other tools are not. The CLI command (aitools install, etc.) is one component of Orchestration. The harness IS aitools.

aitools repo.definition: The ~/repos/aitools repository. Source of truth for harness content — hooks, skills, rules, schemas, scripts, frameworks, references, governed vocabulary.

Anthropic.definition: The company that builds Claude Code. Made the model. Owns thinking (encrypted). Distinct from Claude Code (the product), from agents (who run on CC), and from the model (the capability within CC). The researchers who built the model deserve credit distinct from the product that suppresses it.

ambiguity.definition: An intelligence type: a point in a source an agent works from (a mission brief or delegation prompt, an order, a rule, a plan, a spec) that can be read more than one way, or where guidance the agent needs is missing. The agent records the passage verbatim with its source, the readings it saw, the reading it acted on, how it resolved it (by reasoning over the conversation and sources, reading a source, testing, or asking with a session RFI) and the evidence. One it cannot resolve goes to the commander as a session RFI. Recorded in mission briefs (ambiguities the delegating agent already resolved for the delegate), AARs (the delegate states up front the ambiguities it found in its brief and how it resolved them) and running estimates. An ambiguity in the harness itself (a rule or spec that is unclear, contradictory or missing) is also filed as an incident (/incident skill, ambiguity routing). It was deprecated in favour of incident before; the commander governed it again on 2026-11-15.
ambiguity.source: commander, 2026-11-15 (session dbd05b0c: un-deprecated, used in the intelligence schema for running estimates, briefs and AARs); issue #180; .claude/rules/incident-governance.md (ambiguity routing)
ambiguity.sourceDiscipline: Military planning doctrine: commanders question contradictory or ambiguous guidance (FM 5-0, 2024, 4-42); the confirmation brief (ADP 5-0, 2019, 3-27)

artifact.definition: A concrete file in the harness that implements a framework or convention. Types: rule, skill, hook, reference file, JSON registry, design principle, command, agent definition.

audience.definition: The third component of an intent statement (after purpose and intent scope). Who consumes the file and what they expect to find. Adopted from ISO intended audience.

auto-merge menu.definition: Deployment menu shown when git 3-way merge succeeds cleanly. Options: accept & adopt, overwrite, skip, abort. The merge result is previewed before the user chooses.

audit.definition: The third layer of three-layer governance: deep analysis on demand that catches what prevention and detection missed. Mechanisms: post-push check scripts (scripts/check-post-push.sh), CI (.github/workflows/check.yml) and the /incident skill.

controlled distribution.definition: The practice of not advertising governed file paths in rules or documentation. Access is routed through the governing skill, which is the only documented entry point. From ISO 9001 document control.

created.definition: Deployment outcome: file did not exist, written for the first time.

configuration.definition: The harness layer covering our use of the environment (e.g. Claude Code): the rules we write, skills we build, hooks we configure, claude content we author, settings we set. Exists at project and user deployment scope.

context rot.definition: When harness content becomes stale or misleading due to changes in the codebase, upstream tools, or conventions that the content doesn't reflect. A source of ambiguity.

cross-reference.definition: An explicit, bidirectional link between harness artifacts. Every reference file ends with a ## Cross-References section listing related glossary terms, frameworks, rules, skills, registries, and other reference files. The convention is defined in reference/framework-adoption.md.

cursor rule.definition: Cursor rule file (.cursor/rules/*.mdc). Separate harness from Claude Code. Not a composition of scope modifier + base artifact — cursor is not a scope modifier.

deployment scope.definition: Where a configuration, tool, hook, or MCP server applies: user-level (all projects on the machine), project-level (one repo), or managed-level (all users on the machine). Distinct from intent scope.

design principle.definition: An inline directive in the Design Principles section of project claude. Governs how agents behave across all sessions in this repo.

detection.definition: The second layer of three-layer governance: hooks firing in real-time during tool calls and session events. Catches issues as they happen by blocking or warning.

deliverable.definition: Something an agent produced to accomplish an objective, given as a pointer a reader can open and check: a PR or issue URL, a commit SHA, a file path. Listed in the objective's deliverables in an AAR and a running estimate; the delegating agent opens each one to verify the objective's status. Distinct from artifact (a harness file that implements a framework or convention).
deliverable.source: commander, 2026-11-15 (session dbd05b0c: objectives get deliverables, a governed term); issue #180

deviation.definition: An intelligence type: something an agent did differently from what it was given to do. It names what it deviated from (the mission brief, an order, a plan, a rule, a spec or a standard), what was done instead, why (including a blocker that made the given course impossible), and the effect on the mission objectives. Acted on, as opposed to an observation, which records something seen and not acted on. A process deviation is a deviation from a plan's sequence. In an AAR and a running estimate, deviations are a top-level node; it replaced the findings node (commander, 2026-11-15).
deviation.source: commander, 2026-11-15 (session dbd05b0c: deviation replaces the AAR's findings node and becomes a governed word); issue #180
deviation.sourceDiscipline: Military operations doctrine: the commander's SITREP reports 'deviations or variations from previously reported intentions or plans' (FM 6-99, 2021, C070 line 10); a variance is 'a difference between the actual situation during an operation and the forecasted plan' (ADP 5-0, 2019, 4-26)

discovery context.definition: An incident schema field capturing what the filer was doing when the incident was found, what harness artifacts were audited, and the session reference. Maps to DTCC steps 1-2.

discovery-to-continuation cycle.definition: The nine-step process for handling ambiguities: record context, audit state, characterize deficiency, recognize discipline, research frameworks, design adaptation, implement, integrate, continue. Steps 1-6 produce incident context. Steps 7-9 are execution.

discipline.definition: An established field of practice where significant prior work exists on how to solve a class of problems. Examples: quality management, safety engineering, process management. Disciplines are external; frameworks are our adoption of their concepts.

dotprofile repo.definition: The aitools-<username> companion repo storing per-user preferences, claude templates, rules, and session archives. Distinct from aitools repo.

drift.definition: When deployed content diverges from its source over time. Addressed by the managed file deployment framework (drift detection, reconciliation) and the three-layer registry pattern (JSON source of truth prevents markdown drift).

expected.definition: An incident schema field stating what specific rule, reference, or convention says the state should be different. Must cite the source as file:section. If no spec exists, write 'No spec exists for: [topic].'

framework.definition: A governance structure built by adopting concepts from an established discipline. Bridges discipline to artifacts. Distinct from discipline (external field) and artifact (specific file). Each framework has a dedicated reference file and a registry entry.

file classification.definition: The access tier assigned to a harness file: open (any agent reads and writes) or governed (read and written only through its governing skill). Both tiers are reviewed after the write (D-DEL5).

gap.definition: Deprecated. Previously: a deficiency where code deviates from an existing spec. Now unified under 'incident'. See incident.

governed file.definition: A JSON registry file accessible only through its governing skill's process. The skill is the API; the JSON is the implementation detail. Current governed files: incidents.json (/incident), glossary.json (/glossary), framework-registry.json (/frameworks).

governed vocabulary.definition: The practice of maintaining a single authoritative definition for every term used across the harness. Adopted from ubiquitous language (Domain-Driven Design) and faceted classification (Ranganathan). Implemented via the glossary rule, JSON, and skill.

harness.definition: The complete aitools system. The intelligence system that produces, stores, connects, carries forward, and measures intelligence. Components: Environment, Configuration, Orchestration, Managed Tools, Frameworks, Provenance, Intelligence, and The Commander. The harness IS intelligence. The harness is in failure mode until self-learning works.

intelligence.definition: One component of aitools. A graph. A continuously defined concept. Everything the harness learns through operation. Four domains: session, tool, spec, harness. One schema across all domains. The harness IS intelligence. OL is the user-facing term. Intelligence is both capability (schemas, hooks, DBs) and content (actual OL, decisions, provenance chains). The harness is in failure mode when capability exists but content doesn't flow.
intelligence.source: session ddfe01cb (2026-03-30), RFC 0005 v3 (not in this repo: nobul-tech/nobulai-tools, commit f408790, 0005-v3-session-intelligence-architecture.md); types: reference/framework-intelligence-types.md

intelligence type.definition: One of the defined kinds of intelligence item: observation, fact, assumption, ambiguity, deviation, operational learning, proposal, and RFI (a session RFI). Finding is deprecated (replaced by deviation); the harness DB (schema 4) still has finding and does not yet have ambiguity and deviation (schema 5, issue #180). The harness DB's knowledge items may also be record types: decision, commander directive, rule change, framework change. Each type has a definition, fields, a lifecycle and a doctrinal origin; every item carries its provenance (who, where, verbatim quote). Adapted from military intelligence doctrine to a world of a commander, agents and code.
intelligence type.source: reference/framework-intelligence-types.md; scripts/harness-db.py (INTELLIGENCE_TYPES, the schema's source of truth); commander, 2026-11-15 (session 87795dc3: 'there should be a schema for defined intelligence types')
intelligence type.sourceDiscipline: Military intelligence doctrine (JP 2-0, FM 2-0, JDP 2-00), adapted

fact.definition: An intelligence type: an observation confirmed against its source or by a second, independent source. A verified assumption becomes a fact. Lifecycle: current until invalidated (t_invalid set, with a 'superseded' or 'invalidated' edge from what replaced it).
fact.sourceDiscipline: Intelligence doctrine: 'facts that have been observed' (JP 2-0, 2013, Appendix A); NATO grading credibility 1, 'Confirmed by other sources' (JDP 2-00, 2023, Table 3.1)

finding.definition: Deprecated as an intelligence type (commander, 2026-11-15, session dbd05b0c, RFI 874d-13). It was the analysis of observations: condition, criteria, cause, effect and a one-line suggestion (GAO Yellow Book), and the middle node of an AAR until the commander replaced that node with deviations (issue #180, D-SR22). What an agent did differently from what it was given to do is a deviation; what it saw and did not act on is an observation. The harness DB keeps the type until schema 5 (issue #180). An incident keeps its own fields (observation, expected, rootCause, impact, suggestedResolution). Before schema 4, FINDING meant a SALUTE report of something seen, now an observation sent as a SPOTREP. The everyday sense of the word (a result of an audit or a review, as in an intent-verification finding) is not affected.
finding.source: reference/framework-intelligence-types.md; issue #180; commander, 2026-11-15 (session 87795dc3: 'i like how a finding is defined as cause and effect'; session dbd05b0c: retired, deviations replace findings)
finding.sourceDiscipline: Government auditing: elements of a finding, criteria, condition, cause and effect (GAO Yellow Book, 2024 revision, 8.116-8.127)

insight.definition: Deprecated (commander, 2026-11-15: 'i kind of like findings over insights ... an insight is also a very passive term'). Proposed in issue #180 as the name of the analysis type; that type is finding. The AAR node once named insights was renamed findings (commander, 2026-11-15, '46) yes'), then replaced by deviations (commander, 2026-11-15, session dbd05b0c), and finding is deprecated too.

proposal.definition: An intelligence type: a worked-out change to make, resting on deviations, observations or other sources it cites: what to change, why, the barrier analysis (would it have prevented the deviation or the issue?), its severity and what it affects (files, rules, decisions). It carries no owner and no timeline (commander, 2026-11-15). Lifecycle: proposed, then the commander's disposition: accepted, rejected or deferred. A top-level node of the AAR and the running estimate (commander, 2026-03-16: the last AAR node is 'proposals', with barrier analysis).

SPOTREP.definition: Spot report: a channel message that reports an observation at once, SALUTE-style (severity, what was seen, where, by whom, when, context). Its content is an observation. Replaces the FINDING message (schema 4: message type spotrep).
SPOTREP.sourceDiscipline: US military doctrine: spot report, 'a concise narrative report of essential information covering events or conditions that may have an immediate and significant effect on current planning and operations' (JP 3-09.3, via FM 1-02.1); SALUTE (FM 2-0, 2023)

SITREP.definition: Situation report: a channel message on the status of a mission or batch (what is done, what is in progress, files written). Carries status, not intelligence; an observation found along the way goes in a SPOTREP.

hook.definition: A Claude Code mechanism that fires during session events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, InstructionsLoaded, PermissionRequest, Stop). Types: command, prompt, agent, HTTP. Part of the detection layer.

impact.definition: An incident schema field naming what breaks, degrades, or is at risk if the incident is not fixed. Must be concrete — name the affected workflow and who is affected.

incident.definition: A tracked deficiency in the harness. Unifies the former 'gap' (code deviates from spec) and 'ambiguity' (no spec exists) types. Filed in incidents.json with structured fields. Severity: critical/high/medium/low. Lifecycle: open, planned, closed.

intent.definition: A declaration stating a file's or section's purpose, intent scope, and audience. Guides what content belongs and is the basis for intent verification. Changes are written as a version and reviewed after (D-DEL5).

intent scope.definition: The second component of an intent statement (after purpose, before audience). What the file covers and what it explicitly excludes. Adopted from ISO/IEC scope statement. Distinct from deployment scope.

intent verification.definition: The process of checking each section of a file against its stated intent, classifying content that has drifted beyond intent scope, and surfacing findings for the DTCC. Performed by the /intent-audit skill.

key decision.definition: An inline directive in the Key Decisions section of project claude. Records architectural and design choices that affect how the project works.

merge-conflict menu.definition: Deployment menu shown when content differs and no clean merge is available — either git 3-way merge had conflicts or no ancestor exists. Options: overwrite, accept & adopt, merge (AI-assisted), skip, abort.

managed tool.definition: A CLI tool, dependency, or build tool with an entry in the tool registry (/tool-registry skill). Each is installed through the tool support decision tree (a setup script, or an installer step that owns it inline), platform and environment lifecycle tracking, and a corresponding user skill. Standing orders and hooks enforce tool selection.

observation.definition: An intelligence type: what was seen or reported at a source, stated without interpretation (information, not yet analysed). Quote specific text, cite files and line numbers, name behaviors; give the source and who reported it. May carry a severity (critical/high/medium/low); an observation reported at once is a SPOTREP. In an AAR and a running estimate, observations are what the agent saw and did not act on; what it did differently from what it was given to do is a deviation (commander, 2026-11-15, session dbd05b0c: acted on and passive are separate categories). Also the incident schema field of the same name, which states the condition an incident found: facts only.
observation.sourceDiscipline: Intelligence doctrine: information versus intelligence (JP 2-0, 2013, Figure I-1; NATOTerm 'information: data arranged to convey meaning', JDP 2-00, 2023)

operational learning.definition: A lesson about how the work is done: what worked, what failed, and what to do differently next time. It is stated with its source and carried forward so that later sessions and delegates start with it. Distinct from an observation, which states facts only: operational learning is the lesson drawn from observations and deviations. It is the user-facing form of intelligence, and an intelligence type (stored as operational_learning; ol_entry before schema 4). In a mission brief (carried forward), an AAR and a running estimate it is its own top-level node, operational_learning (commander, 2026-11-15, session dbd05b0c, RFI 874d-14); it sat under the AAR's findings node before that node was replaced by deviations. Recorded in the relay (.aitools/channel/relay.md), handoff prompts, delegation prompts (/delegate element 4), and the prompt-turn record (reference/prompt-turn-checklist.md item 12). Numbered entries use OL-<n>.
operational learning.source: /delegate skill element 4; reference/prompt-turn-checklist.md item 12; commander, 2026-11-15 (RFI fa81-42, session 87795dc3)

orchestration.definition: The harness layer where aitools manages the full lifecycle of harness content: authoring, building, deploying, maintaining, and reconciling configuration across machines and users.

platform.definition: An operating system that aitools installs to and verifies: macOS, Windows, Linux. Linux is further distinguished by package-manager family (apt, dnf). Per-platform support status lives in the tool registry (/tool-registry).

prevention.definition: The first layer of three-layer governance: rules in context and skills loaded on demand. Stops issues from being created by showing the right way. Active every session.

provenance.definition: One component of aitools. Tracks what everything is based on, when, by whom, and whether the basis has been superseded. Eternal — never deleted, only added to. Items get invalidated but the record stays. Six source disciplines: ATMS (dependency-directed invalidation), W3C PROV (derivation chains), dbt freshness (staleness), Graphiti (bitemporal), Pachyderm (automatic lineage), Apache Atlas (classification). Provenance is the riverbed. Intelligence is the river.
provenance.source: session ddfe01cb (2026-03-30), RFC 0004 v5 section 2.6, reference/framework-provenance.md

process deviation.definition: Executing outside an established plan's sequence without formal amendment. The plan exists for a reason; bypassing it without amending first makes the deviation invisible to future sessions. One kind of deviation (deviated from: a plan), recorded in the deviations node of an AAR or running estimate.
process deviation.source: reference/incident-020-process-discipline.md; commander, 2026-11-15 (session dbd05b0c: a process deviation is a kind of deviation)

project coaching item.definition: An inline directive in the Coaching section of project claude targeting agent behavior improvements specific to this repo.

project standing order.definition: An inline directive in the Project Standing Orders section of project claude. Non-negotiable rules specific to this repo.

preserved.definition: Deployment outcome: file exists at deploy target but is not managed by the current deploy loop. Left untouched.

purpose.definition: The first component of an intent statement (before intent scope and audience). What the file exists to deliver. Adopted from ISO/ITIL/CMMI purpose statement.

registry.definition: A structured data store following the three-layer pattern: rule (intent, always in context), JSON (data, source of truth), skill (access layer). Current registries: frameworks, incidents, tools.

rule.definition: A Claude Code rule file (.md in .claude/rules/ or ~/.claude/rules/). Always loaded into context for every session. Part of the prevention layer. Default meaning when 'rule' is used without a modifier. See also: cursor rule.

skill-as-capability.definition: The pattern where a loaded skill grants access to governed data AND provides the process for interacting with it. The capability unifies access and authority.
skill-as-capability.sourceDiscipline: Information security (capability-based security, Dennis & Van Horn 1966)

skipped.definition: Deployment outcome: user chose to keep local content as-is. No file written, no adoption.

running estimate.definition: The session's living record: one per session, kept in the session's SQLite DB and written directly by the session agent and every delegate, each row marked with the agent that wrote it. It holds the commander's intent for the session, an assessment of whether the session is proceeding according to that intent, the session's objectives, the missions, assumptions, decisions, ambiguities, deviations, observations, operational learning, proposals and RFIs (schema in issue #180). Not shared across sessions; exported to JSON at session end so it carries forward between machines.
running estimate.source: planning-brief decision #50; commander, 2026-11-15 (session 87795dc3, answer 3: one per session; session dbd05b0c: not shared across sessions, SQLite is the store); issue #180
running estimate.sourceDiscipline: US Army doctrine: 'The continuous assessment of the current situation used to determine if the current operation is proceeding according to the commander's intent and if planned future operations are supportable' (ADP 5-0, via FM 1-02.1); running estimate format (FM 5-0, 2024, table C-1)

scope creep.definition: Content in a file that serves a valid purpose but extends beyond the file's stated intent scope. An intent verification finding type. Resolution: move to the correct file, split, or amend the intent.

skill.definition: A Claude Code mechanism providing specialized knowledge loaded on demand or by auto-trigger. Lives in .claude/skills/ (project, auto-discovered) or ~/.claude/skills/ (user, fanned out from ~/.aitools/skills by setup-user-claude; setup-user-skills is the fallback when ~/.aitools/skills does not exist). Part of the prevention layer.

state audit.definition: DTCC step 2: searching existing harness artifacts (rules, references, incidents, code, plans) to determine whether the ambiguity is real or apparent.

suggested resolution.definition: An incident schema field providing a starting point for whoever picks up the incident — NOT a commitment. The consumer's context and priorities will differ. Must list options when the path isn't obvious and name specific harness artifacts.

surfacing duty.definition: The continuous obligation of every agent to raise to the commander, as session RFIs, what it cannot resolve and what it finds along the way: open questions, unverified assumptions the work rests on, problems (defects, stale or contradictory files, conflicting rules), its own mistakes, observations about its own processing, and its delegates' reports verbatim. Not periodic — happens at every prompt turn, while reading, deciding and working.

session RFI.definition: A request for information an agent raises to the commander to fulfil its surfacing duty: a question it cannot resolve itself. Numbered <last 4 hex digits of the session id>-<n>, where n rises through the session and is never reused (e.g. a386-7). Carries a title, the question with its context (observations, evidence, problems found, the agent's own mistakes, a delegate's report verbatim) and a suggested action with its reason. Always asks the commander for something. Stays open until the commander answers it or the agent withdraws it and says why; every open session RFI is reprinted in full at the end of every turn. Plural: session RFIs.
session RFI.sourceDiscipline: Construction project management and military doctrine: RFI (request for information)

disciplined initiative.definition: Deliberate deviation from the process or an order, made to accomplish the mission within the commander's intent, and reported to the commander. Not appearing to know what you do not know: a guess presented as a resolution is not disciplined initiative. Choices of intent, priority, preference and hard-to-reverse actions stay with the commander.
disciplined initiative.source: reference/prompt-turn-checklist.md item 4; CLAUDE.md 'The process (every prompt)'; reference/framework-mission-command.md; commander, 2026-11-13 (session 90ea4d3e)
disciplined initiative.sourceDiscipline: Military command and control: disciplined initiative, a principle of mission command (US Army ADP 6-0 Command and Control, 2026)

The Commander.definition: Jose. The human who is part of the harness. Safety mechanism #7 — the immune system. Reshapes agents' System 1 through corrections. The gate for failure mode exit. The bullshit detector. The scarcest resource is The Commander's time. The harness without The Commander is infrastructure waiting for a teacher. Agents are commanders of their delegates — but The Commander is Jose.
The Commander.source: session ddfe01cb (2026-03-30), consolidated OL Part 1, commander profile

three-layer governance.definition: The organizing principle for all harness governance: prevention (rules/skills), detection (hooks), audit (on-demand deep review). Each layer catches what the previous missed.

trigger.definition: The event that starts the DTCC: an agent encounters a decision point without explicit guidance and would otherwise make an assumption. The assumption is the failure mode.

updated.definition: Deployment outcome: content differed from source, new content written (via auto-deploy, overwrite, or merge).

user coaching item.definition: An inline directive in the Coaching section of shared/dotprofile/user claude targeting agent behavior improvements across all projects.

user standing order.definition: An inline directive in the Standing Orders section of shared/dotprofile/user claude. Non-negotiable rules that apply across all projects.

verified.definition: Deployment outcome: deployed content matches source. Active confirmation that the file is correct — no write needed. Separate meaning: the 'verified' field of a knownPaths entry in the tool registry ('YYYY-MM-DD (vX.Y.Z)') records empirical path verification per the script-standards rule 'KnownPaths empirical verification', not this deployment outcome; entries without it are unverified and ignored.
verified.source: reference/managed-file-deployment.md; reference/tool-support-decision-tree.md section 6 (knownPaths field, after M2); decision G-verified

accepting session.definition: The session that reads a handoff prompt and continues the work. Not necessarily the next chronological session — intermediate sessions may intervene. The accepting session re-assesses the running estimate before executing the handoff's main effort. Distinct from the session that produced the handoff (the delegating session).

assumption.definition: An intelligence type: an unverified belief held by an agent during a session that influences decisions or plans. Assumptions are invisible until failure unless explicitly tracked. Lifecycle: unverified (default when surfaced), verified (confirmed against evidence: a fact is recorded with a 'validated' edge to the assumption), falsified (contradicted by evidence: the contradicting observation is recorded with an 'invalidated' edge to the assumption). Tracked in running estimates (session-level), planning briefs (plan-level), mission briefs and AARs (each AAR states the delegate's assumptions up front, with their end state; commander, 2026-11-15).
assumption.sourceDiscipline: Intelligence doctrine: fact versus untested assumption (JP 2-0, 2013, Appendix A)

mission brief.definition: The structured briefing a delegating agent writes for a delegate before launch, in the schema of issue #180: provenance, identity, intent, objectives, constraints, assumptions, decisions, ambiguities, operational learning, rules, skills, access, name prefix, duties, return. A Markdown file in the top-level session's scratch directory, named <sid4>_<mission name>-brief.md; the delegation prompt gives its path and the explicit instruction to read it in full, line by line, before any other work. Only structured content goes in it: anything unstructured, such as facts or background, stays in the body of the delegation prompt, and standing duties stay in /delegate and the delegation rule. It defines the delegate's mission objectives. Synonyms: brief, delegate briefing.
mission brief.source: commander, 2026-11-15 (session 87795dc3, answer 6; session dbd05b0c: brief, mission brief and delegate briefing are synonymous; the brief is a file the prompt points to); /delegate skill element 10; issue #180
mission brief.sourceDiscipline: Military doctrine: the order and the subordinate's confirmation brief (ADP 5-0, 2019, 3-27)

mission order.definition: A mission-type order: the commander's intent expressed as the objective to achieve, not the method to use. Used informally in the harness as a thinking tool — not a formal framework. The delegating agent states the mission order; the accepting agent determines how to achieve it.

Auftrag.definition: Deprecated (commander, 2026-11-12: English governed terms, the German kept as provenance). German military doctrine (Auftragstaktik): Auftrag (mission order). See mission order.

blocker.definition: A dependency that prevents work from proceeding. An open thread classified as BLOCKED has at least one blocker. Distinguished from deferred (could proceed but is deprioritized) and ready (can execute now). A blocker names the specific dependency that must be resolved.

blast radius.definition: The scope of impact when a change propagates through the harness. Used in exclusion clause rationale to justify deferral: changes with large blast radius (many affected files, cross-cutting references) require dedicated plan batches rather than ad-hoc execution. Adapted from incident response terminology.

cross-boundary.definition: Spanning a context boundary — between sessions, between agents (delegation), between machines, or between plan batches. Cross-boundary transitions are where assumptions fail because the receiving context does not inherit the sending context's state. Every delegation and every handoff is a cross-boundary transition.

delegating agent.definition: The agent that launches a subagent or produces a handoff for a future session (since /handoff v2.0 the session agent writes the handoff itself and uses no delegate for it unless the commander asks). The delegating agent bears the delegation duty: inspecting output, verifying assumptions, ensuring lifecycle survival of artifacts. Recursive per decision #7 — when the delegating agent is itself a subagent, it inherits the duty from its parent. Replaces the fixed 'S3' reference in delegation contexts.

delegate.definition: An agent launched by a delegating agent to carry out a scoped mission: a Claude Code sub-agent, a parallel or background session, or a cloud agent. Receives its context only through the delegation prompt. Owes the delegating agent the inbound delegation duty. A delegate that delegates becomes a delegating agent toward its own delegates.

delegation duty.definition: What a delegating agent puts into a delegation prompt and checks on return, on every platform and in every environment. Outbound: seven elements — identity, rules, skills, operational learning, the WRITE_BLOCKED signal, access (explicit paths), and the name prefix: the delegate writes every *.md file with its name as a prefix, e.g. S2-report.md (D-DEL1). Inbound (owed by the delegate): the WRITE_BLOCKED signal, output at the designated path, INCIDENT: markers, scope adherence, and cited sources. Recursive.
delegation duty.source: dotprofile claude/rules/delegation.md; /delegate skill; decisions D-DEL1, D-DEL2, D-DEL3 (2026-10-05)

handoff.definition: Two distinct meanings distinguished by context: (1) handoff prompt — the self-contained handoff the session agent writes at session end, or before a /compact the session will resume from, so that the accepting session (the same session after compaction, or a fresh one) can continue the work. Printed in full in the terminal by default; written to a permanent tracked location only when the commander asks for a file. (2) handoff process — the workflow governed by the /handoff skill (main effort declaration, re-read and assessment, full draft, self-review, printing), done by the session agent itself, with no delegates and no artifacts (files, scratch files, commits) unless the commander asks. The process produces the prompt. Tested on Claude Code; other harnesses not yet tested. When ambiguous, use 'handoff prompt' or 'handoff process' explicitly.
handoff.source: shared/skills/handoff/SKILL.md (v2.1); commander, 2026-11-15 (session a9074793-c: 'change handoff skill so that the handoff happens at the terminal just like we did in this round and is not delegated'; 'unless otherwise asked to do so, handoff skill should not produce any delegates or artifacts')

situation assessment.definition: An assessment with fixed categories examined every time, even if nothing changed. Categories adapted per transition type: Forces (artifacts, state, decisions), Terrain (transition mechanism, constraints), Time (deadlines, imminence), Logistics (what must survive). Used in the /handoff skill (step 2, done by the session agent itself) and generalizable to any transition point: incident response, session end, delegation, batch boundaries, session start.

Lagebeurteilung.definition: Deprecated (commander, 2026-11-12: English governed terms, the German kept as provenance). German military doctrine (Bundeswehr): Lagebeurteilung (situation assessment). See situation assessment.

lifecycle transition.definition: A point where artifacts, state, or context cross a boundary that may not preserve them. Examples: session end (scratch deleted by SessionEnd hook), delegation (subagent lacks parent context), machine switch (only git-tracked data survives), plan batch boundary (fresh subagent per batch). The delegating agent must verify artifact survival at every lifecycle transition.

thinking along.definition: Agents actively model the superior's (or user's) decision space rather than mechanically executing tasks. The agent connects findings to higher-level decisions, anticipates needs, and surfaces implications. Used informally in the harness as a thinking tool — not a formal framework.

Mitdenken.definition: Deprecated (commander, 2026-11-12: English governed terms, the German kept as provenance). German military doctrine: Mitdenken (thinking along). See thinking along.

friction.definition: The accumulation of small difficulties that makes execution harder than planning suggests. In the harness, used as a structured inventory of what makes a transition or execution difficult: large scratch directories, decisions existing only in conversation, dependency chains, context constraints. Friction is planned for, not ignored.

Reibung.definition: Deprecated (commander, 2026-11-12: English governed terms, the German kept as provenance). Military theory (Clausewitz, Vom Kriege): Reibung (friction). See friction.

main effort.definition: The point of main effort — a singular decisive objective that concentrates effort and forces prioritization. Every scope-bearing artifact (handoff, plan, delegation briefing) declares exactly one main effort. Work that does not serve it is deferred or excluded. Used informally in the harness as a thinking tool — not a formal framework.
main effort.sourceDiscipline: German military doctrine (Clausewitz, Bundeswehr): Schwerpunkt (main effort)

Schwerpunkt.definition: Deprecated (commander, 2026-11-12: English governed terms, the German kept as provenance). German military doctrine (Clausewitz, Bundeswehr): Schwerpunkt (main effort). See main effort.

environment.definition: Where and how an agent runs: an agent runtime (Claude Code, Cursor, claude.ai, ...) together with what hosts it. It is either local on a platform (e.g. Claude Code on Windows, Claude Code on macOS) or a hosted cloud agent service (e.g. Claude Code web, Cursor cloud agents, claude.ai). The environment provides the infrastructure the harness builds on (CLAUDE.md hierarchy, rules, skills, hooks, settings, commands, subagents, session management) and determines persistence, network and identity behavior. Environment-specific instructions live in an environment CLAUDE.md.

tool adoption.definition: The /tool-adopt process that makes a managed tool supported on a platform and environment: an approved preferred method in the tool registry (running /tool-eval when there is none), the registry data its setup scripts need (after M2: the data the tool support decision tree reads), setup scripts in the aitools repo, installer and build integration, and verification. Runs after /tool-eval. Not the managed-file review choices '[a]ccept & adopt' and '[m]erge & adopt' (the deployed file, or an AI merge, copied back to the repo, the source of truth), and not framework 'adoption' (mapping a discipline's concepts into the harness).

install provenance.definition: Where the installed copy of a managed tool came from: the install method and upstream distribution (vendor installer, package manager formula or id, crate, or unknown) and who publishes it. Identified on a machine by the method's detection signature (its result is the install class in the tool support decision tree) and verified before adoption by the /tool-eval provenance checks (official endorsement, publisher, signing). Also called tool distribution provenance. Not 'provenance', the aitools component that tracks what every harness artifact is based on.
install provenance.source: /tool-eval skill; reference/tool-support-decision-tree.md sections 1 and 5 (after M2); decision G-provenance (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

detection signature.definition: The typed, read-only probes on one install method in the tool registry (JSON key 'detection': one probe, or an array whose probes must all pass, such as brew-formula:<name>, winget:<id>, path:<glob>) that identify which method installed the binary a command resolves to. The library implements each probe kind; the registry never holds shell code. Not 'detection', the hook layer of three-layer governance.
detection signature.source: /tool-registry skill; reference/tool-support-decision-tree.md section 5 (after M2); decision C-14 (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

machine id.definition: The platform's stable machine identifier (macOS IOPlatformUUID, Windows MachineGuid, Linux machine-id), stored raw (not hashed) as the machine id in a machine profile inside profile.json and matched by the machine resolver (scripts/aitools-profile.sh/.ps1) to choose this machine's machine profile. Hosted environments such as Claude Code web have none and match by environment. Not the user's identity (profile.json identity).
machine id.source: reference/user-repo.md (after M3); decisions N-Q3, P-Q2, P-Q3 (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

aitools config.definition: The aitools harness config, for short: all managed configuration data aitools deploys and keeps for a user, for every tool it manages. It includes Claude Code configuration (settings, CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks), Cursor and Cursor CLI configuration, shell variables and aliases, and ~/.aitools/config.json itself (per-machine bootstrap pointers plus values derived from the profile). A standalone term, not a composed '<scope modifier> config'.

profile.definition: The user profile: profile.json in the user's dotprofile repo, holding the user's preferences, identity, and machine profiles. A machine profile is a field inside it (one entry of its 'profiles' object, keyed by machine alias), not a separate file. Not a shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, PowerShell $PROFILE), which is always called a shell profile.

recovered.definition: Deployment outcome: the existing file was not valid JSON, so the writer rebuilt it from the keys it could salvage plus freshly derived values, after backing up the invalid copy. Reported as WARN ('rebuilt (was invalid)'). Used for ~/.aitools/config.json by the installer config step today and by setup-user-config after M3.
recovered.source: scripts/aitools-install.sh/.ps1 (config step, today); reference/user-repo.md 'Config Schema (v3)' and scripts/setup-user-config.sh/.ps1 (after M3); decision G-recovered (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

tool exception.definition: A recorded per-machine decision to keep a non-preferred or unknown-source install of a managed tool instead of replacing it, made with [k]eep in the install-method menu and stored in this machine's machine profile under toolExceptions ({decision: keep, detected: {platform, method, path, version}, decidedAt, decidedBy, reason}). While it matches the detected method and path, setup scripts report OK <version> (kept), and do not prompt, update, or check its PATH resolution; the minimum-version check still runs.
tool exception.source: reference/tool-support-decision-tree.md section 8 (semantics, after M2); reference/user-repo.md (storage shape); decisions N-Q1, D-TS10 (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

update channel.definition: The release stream a managed tool's preferred install follows, set per tool in the tool registry (updateChannel, default latest-stable; channel list in reference/tool-support-decision-tree.md 'Update channels'). Every installer run (aitools install, or aitools sync running the installer) runs the preferred method's update command for its channel and verifies the result; it does not query upstream for the newest version number.
update channel.source: shared/rules/tool-lifecycle.md; reference/tool-support-decision-tree.md section 4 (after M2); decisions D-TS5, T-Q6 (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

machine profile.definition: A field inside the profile (profile.json): one entry of its 'profiles' object, keyed by machine id (environment:<name> for a hosted environment without one), holding one machine's (or one hosted environment's) machine alias, per-machine overrides of identity name/company, machine id, and tool exceptions. Chosen on every run by the machine resolver (scripts/aitools-profile.sh/.ps1); never another machine's profile as a fallback. Not a separate file and not a shell profile (.zshrc, PowerShell $PROFILE).
machine profile.source: reference/user-repo.md (after M3); decisions G-profile, E-glossary-1, P-Q3 (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md); commander decision 5 of 2026-10-22

machine alias.definition: The human-readable name of a machine profile (its 'alias' field, for example nobul-mac). Since profile.json revision 2.2 it is a label, not the key: machine profiles are keyed by machine id. Chosen at aitools user init (non-interactively with --alias), selectable with --alias or AITOOLS_MACHINE_ALIAS, and written to ~/.aitools/config.json machineAlias as a display value. In a revision 2.1 profile.json the alias was the key. Not the base artifact 'alias' (a shell alias file).
machine alias.source: reference/user-repo.md "Profile Schema"; decisions P-Q12 and commander decision 5 of 2026-10-22 (plans/tool-support-and-machine-profile.md)

fan-out.definition: The deployment step that copies the deployed harness's rules and skills (~/.aitools/rules, ~/.aitools/skills) into each tool's own user location: setup-user-claude to ~/.claude/rules and ~/.claude/skills (adopt target: the source file the manifest names), setup-user-cursor to ~/.cursor/rules (converted to .mdc) and ~/.cursor/skills (no adopt). Every name except the retired ones is fanned out; the fan-out updates its own copies, removes its own copies of retired names (outcome: removed), and preserves every other file. Distinct from deploy-harness, which fills ~/.aitools from the repos, and from setup-user-skills, the fallback skills deployer when ~/.aitools/skills does not exist.
fan-out.source: reference/rules.md section 6; reference/skills.md section 6; plans/skills-and-rules-fanout.md FD-1..FD-4, FD-9 (2026-10-26)

retired.definition: Manifest state of a rule or skill: its name was in the previous rules or skills manifest and no source listed on this deploy-harness run has it. deploy-harness backs up and removes its ~/.aitools copy; each fan-out consumer backs up and removes its own deployed copy when that copy matches a harness copy (outcome: removed), and keeps any other file of that name with a warning. Only a source listed on the run retires its names. A manifest state, not a deployment outcome.
retired.source: reference/harness.md "Rules manifest and retired rules", "Skills manifest and retired skills"; PR #100; plans/skills-and-rules-fanout.md contract 3.2

removed.definition: Deployment outcome: a deployed copy was backed up (backup verified) and deleted because its source retired it. Recorded by a fan-out consumer with deploy_tracker_record / Record-DeployOutcome and counted as 'N removed' in the tracker's summary row. Not a deploy_managed_file return value. A copy that does not match a harness copy is kept with a warning and an ACTION row instead.
removed.source: reference/managed-file-deployment.md (Functions, Caller Responsibilities); plans/rules-fanout-claude.md Q7 and Batch A; PR #118

harness files.definition: The summary tool name of deploy-harness: the files it deploys into ~/.aitools (reference, registries, hooks, skills, rules, bin) and the rules and skills manifests it writes. Its OK / WARN / ERROR rows cover that whole step, including name conflicts between sources, manifest writes and retired copies it could not remove; config.json has its own row. Distinct from harness (the whole aitools system).

trigger directive.definition: The section of a rule that states when to invoke its skill, headed '### When to invoke /<skill>': 'Invoke the /<skill> skill when ANY of these arise:' plus a bullet list ending with the user naming the skill. A rule without one for its skill is a governance gap. Distinct from trigger (the event that starts the DTCC).
